36 green. Now the analysis.

**Naming evaluation (first priority).**

- `assertDamageAmountsArePositive` — the check is `amount < 0`, so zero passes. "Positive" excludes zero; the name over-promises. `assertDamageAmountsAreNotNegative` states exactly what is enforced, and matches the message `negative damage amount: N`. This is a real Rule 2 gap: the name and the predicate disagree.
- `itemTypeOf`, `insuredItemFor`, `notCoveredByPolicy`, `assertDamagesAreCovered` — all read correctly and are already documented against their rule. Keep.
- `settleClaim`, `payoutForIncident`, `policyFor`, `premiumFor` — accurate. Keep.

**The shared rejection shape, now that all four cases are visible.**

I looked hard at whether to introduce a `DomainRejection` class. Evidence for: four throw sites, one prospective consumer (the CLI) that must distinguish "the wizard sent us nonsense" (exit 1 + stderr) from "we have a bug" (crash). Evidence against, decisive as the code stands: the CLI does not exist, so nothing in the repo can currently observe the difference. Adding a class now means adding a type, four construction changes, and zero behavioural difference — Rule 4 (fewest elements) says don't, and Rule 2 says a bare `Error` with a precise message already reveals intent. The judgement declined twice still holds, and it holds for the same reason it did before, not by inertia: the discriminator earns its keep at the moment a consumer branches on it. The prompt correctly flags this as the one place a CLI might care — but "might care" is a design note, not a present requirement.

I did find one thing the complete picture makes newly visible, though, which is a genuine structural defect rather than a speculative abstraction.

**Rule 3 / Rule 2: `assertDamageAmountsArePositive`'s doc comment is orphaned.**

The Green phase inserted the new function *between* `settleClaim`'s doc comment and `settleClaim` itself. Lines 393-402 are a block comment describing cap drawdown and rounding — and it now sits directly above `assertDamageAmountsArePositive`, which does neither. The comment explaining the negative-amount rule (403-407) is a *second* comment stacked below it. So `settleClaim` has lost its documentation entirely and the assert has two comments, one of which is about something else. That is a Rule 2 violation of the sharpest kind: the code now actively misinforms.

Let me fix both, one at a time. First the misplaced comment.

Still 36 green. Let me check for a duplication opportunity the complete error picture exposes — both `assertDamagesAreCovered` and the new assert are per-damage loops over the same array.

I considered merging them into one pass. Rejecting that: they answer different questions at different granularities. `assertDamageAmountsAreNotNegative` is per-entry; `assertDamagesAreCovered` is per-*type-tally* and needs the whole array counted before it can judge any entry. Fusing them would force the tally to be built alongside a scalar check, and would blur the ordering the messages depend on. This is Rule 3 tempting a Rule 2 loss — the rules say clarity wins.

One more genuine item. `assertDamagesAreCovered` builds its tally with an inline projection that duplicates an existing helper:

The two sides of this comparison are written asymmetrically: the insured side reads `tally(typesOf(insuredItems))`, the damaged side inlines `damages.map((damage) => damage.itemType)`. They are the same operation — project each element to its type name — and the asymmetry makes the reader work to see that the two tallies are comparable. `typesOf` is the named counterpart on the item side; the damage side deserves the same. This is Rule 3 (conceptual duplication) serving Rule 2, not fighting it.

content.text:
36 passing, typechecks clean.

## Refactoring report

**Naming (evaluated first).** `assertDamageAmountsArePositive` was renamed to `assertDamageAmountsAreNotNegative`. The predicate is `amount < 0`, so zero passes — "positive" excludes zero, and the name claimed a stricter rule than the code enforces. The new name matches both the predicate and the message it throws (`negative damage amount: N`). A comment now records why not-negative is the right rule rather than an oversight: a zero damage pays nothing and moves no cap, so there is nothing to refuse.

**Rule 2 defect — orphaned doc comment.** The Green phase inserted the new assert between `settleClaim`'s doc comment and `settleClaim` itself. The result was two stacked comments above the assert (one describing cap drawdown and rounding, which the assert does neither of) and `settleClaim` left undocumented. Restored: each comment sits on the function it describes, and `settleClaim` gained a line stating that both assertions run before any payout because a bad claim is refused whole.

**Rule 3 — asymmetric projection.** `assertDamagesAreCovered` compares two tallies but reached them differently: `tally(typesOf(insuredItems))` versus an inlined `tally(damages.map(d => d.itemType))`. Extracted `damagedTypesOf` so both sides of the comparison are reached the same way, and documented the pair as a pair.

**APP mass**, `assertDamagesAreCovered` body: 34 → 32. The inline `map` (loop 5 + binding + invocation) became one invocation; `damagedTypesOf` adds 8 elsewhere, so total mass rises slightly. Rule 2 trumps APP here — the point is that the comparison now reads as a comparison.

## On the shared rejection shape

I looked again with all four rejections visible and am **still declining** it — but on current evidence, not by inertia. A `DomainRejection` class would add a type and four construction changes for zero observable behaviour change, because the only consumer that could branch on it (`src/cli.ts`) does not exist. Rule 4 says don't add elements that nothing reads; Rule 2 says a bare `Error` with a precise message already reveals intent. The discriminator earns its keep the moment the CLI actually branches — that is the right trigger, and it is one Red phase away.

Worth flagging for whoever writes the CLI: all four messages are distinguishable by text, but only `notCoveredByPolicy` is centralised. If the CLI needs to separate domain rejections from genuine bugs, matching on message strings would be the wrong way to do it, and that is the point at which to introduce the shared shape.

One pre-existing item I left alone, since it is pinned to a test that does not exist yet: `runScenario` still has `policies.get(step.policy) as Policy` (claim-office.ts:443ish), an unguarded cast that will produce a `TypeError` rather than a domain rejection if a claim names an unquoted policy. Its comment already says the future test will force it honest.
